newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Thousands in south Albania denounce government.
newsitem.headline: Thousands in south Albania denounce government.

text.p: Thousands of Albanian investors duped by pyramid investment schemes marched through the centre of this southern port city on Wednesday to demand refunds and the resignation of the right-wing government.

About 3,000 marchers denouncing President Sali Berisha converged on Flag Square in the centre of the rubbish-strewn Adriatic port less than two weeks after riots swept the Balkan state after the collapse of pyramid funds.
Cordons of riot police watched nervously over Wednesday's demonstration but did not intervene.
"Down with the government, down with Sali Berisha," shouted the protesters, who vowed to remain in the square for at least five days and then organise a march on the capital Tirana.
"The government has just kept on lying to us," said Besim Aliaj, one of many demonstrators who had invested money earned while working in Italy. He said he had tied up the equivalent of $170,000.

Investors in Europe's poorest country have already begun receiving partial compensation of their stakes in two of five failed schemes. But the refunds were marked by confusion and many people were turned away from payout points.
Banks were issuing refunds in the capital Tirana, where there was no indication of tension.
Enraged depositors set fire to public buildings last month in several Albanian towns. Protests were particularly violent in Vlore and other towns in the more volatile south of the Balkan country.
But a police crackdown and the threat of long jail terms for public order offences had kept many would-be protesters away from planned demonstrations last weekend.
Authorities had feared a resumption of unrest in the south after the head of the Gjallica investment scheme popular in the region announced on Tuesday that he was broke.
Newspapers reported that between $350 million to $500 million was tied up in the Gjallica fund. More than $1 billion is believed to be invested in all the various pyramids.
Police set up roadblocks on approaches to Vlore and refused to let through cars with out-of-town registrations.

The Tirana daily Koha Jone said 900,000 investors in the Gjallica scheme had sent a petition to Berisha demanding that he sell one of two state hydroelectric stations in northern Albania and pay them off with the proceeds.
In the six years after the fall of eastern Europe's most repressive communist regime, virtually every family in the country of 3.4 million had poured money into pyramid schemes.

Banks have announced that 150,000 investors in the Populli scheme would receive 60 percent of their deposits. A further 200,000 with money tied up in the Xhaferri programme were due to receive even less -- 52 percent.
Berisha, speaking after round table talks on Tuesday boycotted by most opposition parties, offered help to worst-hit depositors, particularly those who sold homes to pump money into the schemes.
But he said the government could not fuel inflation by promising more than it was able to provide.
Berisha's Democratic Party retained power last May in elections denounced by observers as fraudulent.
He rejects charges that his government failed to warn investors about pyramid programmes, under which interest to older investors is paid out with deposits from new customers.
